summary: Describes a file format for storing flow data based on IPFIX. It lists requirements for binary flow files and defines the IPFIX File format using IPFIX Messages.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic records are usually sent live. This says how to save them neatly in a file so you can open them later.

questions: what is the ipfix file format
how to store ipfix flow data in a file
how to sign an ipfix file
subtitle: A standard way to save network flow records in a file by reusing the IPFIX message format.

tldr.problem: Network flow data is stored in ad hoc formats such as raw NetFlow datagram dumps, which are hard to extend, describe and standardize, while XML is too bulky for billions of flows per hour.
tldr.mechanism: An IPFIX File is simply a stream of IPFIX Messages written to a filesystem. Extra file metadata such as checksums, time windows and session details is carried with IPFIX Options, and signing and compression are done by wrapping the file.
tldr.outcome: Flow tools can share one encoding on the wire and on disk, with CMS detached signatures for integrity and bzip2 or gzip for compression. It is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted.

today: RFC 5655 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the IPFIX File format.

sections.title: Why a Flow File Format Is Needed
sections.content:
Flow data is stored for many reasons and for very different lengths of time. A file may hold the flows for one security investigation and be passed between incident handlers, or it may be a published research dataset kept for months or years, much as libpcap packet traces are. Operational systems also keep long-term archives of flow data.

The RFC argues for flat binary files instead of a relational database, because a database's internal structures are private to one implementation and flow data is not semantically complicated. It also rejects two existing options. A common ad hoc approach is to dump raw Cisco NetFlow datagrams into files, which is understood but not extensible beyond the NetFlow data model. XML is heavyweight and needs a full parser, which matters when datasets can hold millions or billions of flows per hour.

The conclusion is to use the IPFIX Message format itself. It was designed for flow export, is extensible unlike ad hoc dumps and compact unlike XML, and lets implementers reuse the same code for transport and storage.
sections.plainLanguage: People were saving traffic records in messy home-made ways or in huge wordy files. The authors say: use the neat format the records already travel in.

sections.title: Requirements for Flow Storage
sections.content:
The RFC lists what a good flow file format should offer and says how an IPFIX-based file meets each need.

  • Record format flexibility: IPFIX Templates describe each record, and an IANA registry plus enterprise-specific Information Elements allow new fields.
  • Self-description: Templates with only IANA-assigned elements can be fully interpreted. Private elements need the type options defined in RFC 5610.
  • Compression: IPFIX has none, so it is met by wrapping the file (Section 10).
  • Indexing: only limited support, such as a time window or the technique in RFC 5473.
  • Error recovery, authentication and confidentiality: left mostly to lower layers, with optional checksums and CMS signatures added.
  • Anonymization: not supported, because anonymization is still an open area of research.
  • Auditability and replay: met with Options that record session and per-message details.

On performance, the RFC admits that a full analysis needs more implementation experience.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a shopping list for a good filing system: it should hold many kinds of notes, explain itself, shrink down, and stay safe. Most items come from reusing existing tools.

sections.title: Design Overview and Core Rules
sections.content:
An IPFIX File is a serialized stream of IPFIX Messages. Any message stream that would be valid over SCTP, TCP or UDP counts as an IPFIX File, and a File Reader MUST accept it. The filesystem is treated as another, possibly high-latency, IPFIX transport. A File Writer behaves as an IPFIX Exporting Process and a File Reader behaves as a Collecting Process, except where this RFC changes that.

Files contain only IPFIX Messages. Metadata lives in Options inside those messages, so no protocol extension is needed.

Readers MUST accept messages that mix Template Sets, Options Template Sets and Data Sets, accept repeated Template definitions (the new one replaces the old), and accept Template Withdrawals. A single file SHOULD be treated as one Transport Session and MUST NOT be treated as several.

Writers SHOULD store the Templates needed to decode the data inside the file, put each Template before the data it describes, and write messages in ascending Export Time order. They SHOULD use Template Withdrawals only when Template IDs must be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow file is just the same messages that would be sent over the network, saved one after another. The reader reads them like a person who got them live.

sections.title: Writing Files for Different Jobs
sections.content:
The RFC gives extra guidance for particular situations.

  • Beside a Collecting Process: a writer that joins a running session SHOULD first write all the active Templates. To keep session details such as addresses and protocols, it SHOULD store one Transport Session per file and record the details with the Export Session Details Options Template. If it must add data to a message, it SHOULD lengthen the message, and otherwise split it into two roughly equal messages.
  • Beside a Metering Process: exporter and collector elements are meaningless here. This is the only way to give positive authentication of a Metering Process through signatures.
  • Archival storage: a writer MAY spread one session across several files, but MUST also offer a one-file-per-session option. Archival writers SHOULD support compression.
  • Documents: a file used as a document MUST be readable as a single session and self-contained, aside from any detached signature.
  • Testing and diagnostics: files may deliberately break the rules to test collectors and MUST NOT be given to readers that are not under test. Files can also dump flow tables for device debugging.

Tools that split or join files SHOULD write all needed Templates and Options to each output file, and a join must avoid Template ID collisions.
sections.plainLanguage: Different jobs need slightly different habits: keep a diary of who sent the data, make archives that can be split up, or make a test file with mistakes put in on purpose. The rules say how to do each safely.

sections.title: File Metadata with Options Templates
sections.content:
Four Options Templates carry file metadata, and readers and writers SHOULD support them.

  • Message Checksum: attaches an MD5 checksum to a message using messageScope and messageMD5Checksum. It MAY be used when integrity matters but signing is unavailable. The record MUST appear only once per message.
  • File Time Window: gives the earliest flow start and latest flow end using sessionScope, a minFlowStart* element and a maxFlowEnd* element. A writer MUST NOT write more than one time window record per file, and no flow may fall outside the window.
  • Export Session Details: records exporter and collector addresses, ports, certificates, transport protocol and the first and last Export Time. It SHOULD appear only once per file.
  • Message Details: records per-message details such as the collection time, so that several sessions can share one file.

The RFC also defines new Information Elements for these templates, such as collectionTimeMilliseconds (ID 258), messageMD5Checksum (ID 262) and opaqueOctets (ID 266). The MD5 checksum is calculated with the checksum field set to zero. MD5 is judged acceptable because this is a simple checksum, not a security feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Sticky notes on the file: a checksum so you can tell if a page got damaged, the dates the records cover, and where they came from.

sections.title: Signing Files with CMS
sections.content:
To protect integrity and identify the writer, files SHOULD be signed with a CMS detached signature from RFC 3852. The signature is stored in a separate file named like the IPFIX File with .p7s added, so a reader that does not care about signatures can ignore it and the IPFIX File itself is unchanged.

The signature file must contain a ContentInfo that wraps SignedData. Both SignedData and SignerInfo versions MUST be 3, the encapsulated content type is id-data, and eContent MUST be absent because the signature is detached. The certificate profile is that of RFC 5280, and there is only one signer except when keys or algorithms are being changed.

The RFC does not define a method for encrypting files, on the grounds that application needs outweigh interoperability there. It only advises that writers SHOULD use an encryption scheme that can resynchronize after bit errors, such as a block cipher in CBC mode.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is a seal kept in a separate envelope. If you do not care about the seal you ignore it, and the file is exactly as it was.

sections.title: Compression and Error Recovery
sections.content:
Flow data compresses well, so writers and readers SHOULD support compression. Two formats are allowed. Readers and writers that support compression MUST support bzip2 and SHOULD support gzip. bzip2 compresses better and, being a block algorithm, recovers from errors better, while gzip is faster.

Readers SHOULD detect the format from the first bytes, listed in the table below. Because one bit error in a stream-compressed file could lose the whole file, bzip2 is RECOMMENDED where error resilience matters.

After a damaged block, a reader can resynchronize in four steps: find the next 0x00 0x0A, treat it as a candidate message and read its length, check that the bytes after the candidate are again 0x00 0x0A (or end-of-file), and otherwise resume the search two bytes further on. With random data this misidentifies a non-message about 1 in 2^32 times.
sections.plainLanguage: Files can be squashed to save room. If a squashed file gets a scratch, the reader looks for the next message start and checks it lines up before continuing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC builds on the security guidance of RFC 5101, which is mostly about TLS and DTLS protecting exported messages, and uses CMS signatures to give equivalent integrity protection for files.

Files built from data received over TLS or DTLS SHOULD be signed and SHOULD be encrypted out of band, since storing such data unencrypted may breach confidentiality. A gap remains when a File Writer sits beside a Collecting Process: the exporter's identity is not asserted in the file and records could change between the collector and writer. A collocated writer SHOULD NOT sign a file unless the session used TLS or DTLS and the exporter was identified by certificate. Collocating the writer with the Metering Process approximates end-to-end integrity.

For long-term archives, cryptographic strength depends on how long data is kept, so files may need to be re-signed and re-encrypted with stronger keys, wrapping the old protection inside the new. RFC 4810 discusses this.
sections.plainLanguage: A seal only proves who sealed the box, not who packed it. If the packer cannot be trusted, put the sealing machine as close to the source as possible.

items.label: bzip2
items.desc: The string "BZh". Readers and writers MUST support it if they support compression.

items.label: gzip
items.desc: Readers and writers SHOULD support it.

items.label: IPFIX File
items.desc: The version bytes of the first IPFIX Message header, so the file is uncompressed.
